label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: One tool and one empty project, with nothing private in it.
findings.why: As a first-build finisher I do not know which tool, or why 'nothing private' matters, so the first step is one I cannot yet take tomorrow.

findings.quote: when it must stop and ask you
findings.why: I like the idea but have no picture of what a page of rules looks like, so I cannot write mine.

findings.quote: share one brief, one board and one hold
findings.why: Board and hold are used here with no explanation, and they sound like jargon that makes the book feel meant for programmers.

findings.quote: Read it the whole way through, or take the short way
findings.why: It tells me how to read; a plain offer of the two routes would not instruct me.

findings.quote: I keep the time and the plan.
findings.why: Nine one-line hellos in a row read as a list I skim, and I cannot yet tell the roles apart.

findings.quote: These five steps are what I would tell a friend
findings.why: The five steps are then listed at line 9 and drawn again as a path at line 15, so the same thing is said three times.

findings.quote: it is not the usual arrangement
findings.why: Two paragraphs of explaining the narrator before any story made me impatient, as I came for the next step.

findings.quote: from an empty repository a little after midnight
findings.why: 'Repository' is used before it is explained and, as a non-coder, it is the word that tells me this may not be for me.

findings.quote: the slides became data: one file that the presentation read
findings.why: Black Hat Europe, VoiceDebrief and ruv.sgit.ai arrive in one paragraph with no hook for a newcomer, and 'beats' and 'timeline' are unexplained.

findings.quote: There is one more thing I want you to see as you read.
findings.why: It directs what I should see; stating the fact would do.

findings.quote: So let us go through it together.
findings.why: It repeats the invitation already made at line 9 ('what I would do with it if I were you').
The chapter title and the 'Words for this page' note never say what git is, and with 'vaults', 'commits', 'slot' and 'wakes' I felt this was for programmers.

findings.quote: It wrote a short letter, as a file, and put it in the other's mailroom.
findings.why: A run of short sentences describing the letter, one after another, reads as a list; the sequence is clear but choppy.

findings.quote: two public vaults: folders any member could read, synced between their sessions
findings.why: Vaults and 'synced' are new words I have to carry, and the next sentence then says the book team does it differently.
A run of short fragments; it is charming, but it is the third such run on the page.

findings.quote: One note followed, one not, and both are in the record.
findings.why: The deck-to-ruv-sgit note is told in full at line 58 and again at line 90, and the third letter is retold, so I met the scene twice.

findings.quote: which is the point: a disagreement that is written down
findings.why: It leans on 'the point' and a neat contrast to land the idea, which I would take without the flourish.

what_holds: 00-start-here.md: five steps on one page is exactly what I wanted, short and doable, and the 'friend' framing is warm.
00b-who-is-telling-this-story.md: the promise that the agents disagree with the narrator and he keeps the line anyway made me curious.
10-talking-through-git.md: the three-letters scene is easy to follow, the idea that nobody needs to be awake together is clear, and 'a letter is a file' is something I could do tomorrow.
notes: As a first-build finisher I got the factory idea (agents leaving each other files) but only by ignoring words like repository, git, vault, commit and slot. I would start tomorrow with steps 1 to 4 on page one; chapter 10's 'Something to try' is the only place I felt a step I could take.
